summary: Describes how GSS-API domain-based service principal names are mapped onto Kerberos V principal names. It is the Kerberos mechanism companion to the general domain-based names specification. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines how a domain-based GSS-API service name maps to a Kerberos V principal name. It specifies the component order, the realm source, and how internationalized domain names are represented.

questions: how do gss-api domain-based names map to kerberos
what is a kerberos principal name
how does a gss-api service name map to kerberos
subtitle: Maps domain-based GSS-API service names into Kerberos V principal names.

tldr.problem: The Kerberos V GSS-API mechanism needs a rule for mapping service, hostname, and domain parts into a Kerberos principal.
tldr.mechanism: The service, hostname, and domain become the first three principal components, and the realm corresponds to the domain treated as a hostname.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends a particular Kerberos name type and requires ACE-encoded internationalized names in the hostname and domain slots.

today: RFC 5179 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Mapping the Name Components
sections.content:
For a domain-based service name, the service becomes the first Kerberos V principal component, the hostname the second, and the domain the third. The realm corresponds to the domain name treated as a hostname.

The RFC says the same name-canonicalization considerations used elsewhere in Kerberos V and its GSS-API mechanism apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The input has three parts, and each has a defined place in the Kerberos principal. The domain also determines the realm.

sections.title: Kerberos Name Type
sections.content:
Implementations SHOULD use the Kerberos V name type NTT-SRVT-HST-DOMAIN, whose value is 12. They MAY use NT-UNKNOWN instead.

The RFC gives examples of LDAP and kadmin service names mapped to Kerberos principal forms.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives a preferred name-type label and allows an unknown-type label as an alternative.

sections.title: Internationalized Names and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says it is unclear how best to handle internationalization because the Kerberos V core internationalization work was incomplete. For interoperability, implementations MUST use ACE-encoded internationalized domain names in the hostname and domain slots.

For security, the realm of a domain-based principal name must be derived from the hostname rather than the input domain-name slot, as stated in the RFC's security section.
sections.plainLanguage: Internationalized domain names use an encoded form in these name parts. The RFC also specifies which input part must determine the realm.
